blurb: Long scarlet trumpets ranged up a slender stalk, built for hummingbird beaks and mobbed by them. It is a biennial — a flat rosette of finely divided leaves the first year, the flowering spike the second — so it carries on by seeding rather than by persisting.
water: Low; xeric — well-drained ground, little or no supplemental water once established
spread: Single flowering stalk from a basal rosette; reseeds readily
seasons: Scarlet (sometimes pink or white) trumpets through summer on a slender spike; a low rosette in its first year
wildlife: Native bees and butterflies work the flowers

care.hardiness: CSU lists this as a Colorado native plantable to about 9,000 ft, so cold is not the constraint at Boulder's zone 5b–6a.[1]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, into ground prepared to suit it (see Soil). Set out young container plants — most of these natives resent having an established root system disturbed — and water them in well, then taper off.[1][2]
care.sun: Full sun, which is CSU's exposure rating for it.[1]
care.soil: Well-drained soil, lean and gritty. It is a plant of dry open slopes and clearings; the rosette rots in wet ground over winter, which is the usual way gardeners lose it.[1]
care.water: Low. CSU rates its moisture requirement low, and on the semi-arid Front Range that is the number that matters most — the commonest way to kill a xeric native here is kindness with the hose.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space to suit its mature spread of 8–12 in wide. A rosette of finely divided leaves throwing trumpet-shaped flowers that attract hummingbirds — CSU notes it is a biennial and reseeds readily.[1]
care.propagation: By seed, which is how nearly all of these natives are raised and how they persist in a planting. Autumn sowing outdoors lets winter provide the chilling most of them want.[1]
care.bloom: Flowers roughly June through mid-August; CSU records the colour as red, pink, white and the height as 12–30 in tall.[1]
care.maintenance: Treat it as a self-renewing colony, not a clump. Because it is biennial, the way to keep it is to let some seed fall every year — deadhead everything and you will have no plants in two years' time. Sow a patch two years running to get overlapping generations, then leave it alone.[1]
care.troubles: Few pests or diseases when it is sited right. Crown and root rot in soil that stays wet is the usual cause of failure for a Colorado native in a Front Range garden, and it is a siting problem rather than bad luck.[1][2]

references.name: CSU Extension — Native Herbaceous Perennials for Colorado Landscapes (fact sheet 7.242, PDF: complete Table 1)
CSU Extension — Xeriscaping: Perennials and Annual Flowers (7.231)

edible.summary: No documented culinary use; grown as a native hummingbird plant.[1]
edible.caution: No authority consulted documents a food use for scarlet gilia, so this guide treats it as inedible — don't eat it. No part is recorded as notably poisonous. If you meet it in the wild, leave the seedheads: as a biennial it depends entirely on setting seed, so stripping a stand is how you remove it from a site.[1]
